messages.text: I went to a drop-in wheel-throwing class on my own this afternoon, the first time I have touched clay since school. My bowl collapsed twice, and the teacher, Ines, who had clay right up to her elbows, finally came over and had me make a very small cup instead.
Two collapses and then a small cup. Starting smaller is how most people get one to stand.

The cup leans to one side like it is listening to something. I picked a glaze called seafoam and they will fire it next week. My forearms are aching already, and I have not felt this pleased with myself in months.
A cup that leans in to listen, in seafoam. The aching arms sound well earned.
Signed Milo up for the Saturday ceramics club at the community centre this week. There were only twelve places, and I was refreshing the page at seven in the morning to get one.
Seven in the morning for one of twelve places. That is a keen parent and, with luck, a keen potter.
First session today. He rolled out a coil pot, got bored, and turned it into a dinosaur with a very long neck. He carried it to the car on a paper plate as though it were a wedding cake.
A coil pot that grew a neck. And carried with all the ceremony it deserved.
Didn't I tell you once about a time I had a go at pottery myself? How did that go? I can barely remember it now.

Yes, you did — a Saturday evening in June, about three months back. You'd gone to a drop-in wheel-throwing class on your own that afternoon, the first time you'd touched clay since school, and your bowl collapsed twice before Ines, the teacher, who had clay right up to her elbows, came over and had you make a very small cup instead. The cup leaned to one side, you said, like it was listening to something, and you'd picked a seafoam glaze for it, with firing the following week. Your forearms were already aching, and you said you hadn't felt that pleased with yourself in months.
